hints.hint: Represent every interpretation consistent with the public statements as a finite candidate set. For each speaker, group candidates by the value that speaker privately knows. A claim of not knowing deletes groups whose relevant coordinate is already unique. Apply the announcements in chronological order, recomputing information sets after every deletion; do not reason from the original set after later statements. The surviving candidate determines the requested quantity.

Divide by the appropriate power of the variable and set w=(z-1)/z. The equation restricts w to a finite set on a circle. Solve the Möbius relation for z and characterize the image locus geometrically or by an equation in x and y. Use all roots and check exceptional values before extracting the requested circle parameter.

Only a boxed value written after your reasoning block closes is graded, so a trace that never closes scores zero. Close the reasoning as soon as you hold one exact value plus one confirming check. Then write the boxed value as the very first thing after closing, and put any explanation after the box, never before it, so being cut off costs nothing. Never restart the derivation in the write-up. Do not reopen a settled value; only a finished rival computation beats it, unease does not. Set up in coordinates first and write each object's extent; do not assume one figure sits inside another. If a rotation or offset stays free, ask whether the answer depends on it: a symmetry swapping congruent pieces makes every allowed value give the same result, so use the easiest one. For coverings, covered = sum of parts - overlap.

When each term of a required linear pattern may come from any member of a finite menu of fixed-degree polynomials fed consecutive integers, do not difference terms across different polynomials. Because inputs are consecutive, index and input are interchangeable, so every value equals one shared affine L(x)=A+Bx of its own input. Group inputs by which polynomial produced them: each is a root of P(x)-L(x), nonzero of degree deg P since subtracting an affine map keeps the leading term, so a polynomial serves at most deg P inputs, one more forcing P=L. The quantity wanted is the total count of inputs, so sum that capacity across the whole menu, never reporting one factor alone; attain it by letting each polynomial match L on its own block.

Make each stated condition an equation; pin unknown constants first, then verify. Assume nothing unstated. Use the given relation to express remaining unknowns through one variable, then impose the defining equation. Reject roots outside the domain or repeating a known point. A zero or impossible intermediate means relabel, not restart. Box the first candidate meeting every condition.

Model relay-through-a-buffer stack tasks as stack shunting: fix one stated labeling (name items bottom-to-top), keep the ordered source, buffer, and destination stacks, and describe a run by its word of pushes and pops. Restate the target event as a condition on that word, using that a destination stack's bottom is whatever arrived first and its top whatever arrived last, so "lands at the bottom" constrains the earliest moves, not the latest. Never assume all n! final orders or all words are equally likely: stack rules make many orders unreachable and forced moves make branches unequal, so a bare 1/k or 1/k! is a red flag. Multiply true per-step probabilities along each admissible word, using one when a move is forced (empty buffer forces a push, empty source forces a pop) and one half only at free steps; check branch probabilities from each state sum to one.

Numbers before symbols: set the huge parameter to 2, then 3, then 4, solve each tiny integer system by elimination, record the asked value. Divide consecutive entries, tracking signs separately; that ratio exposes the rule. Never build a polynomial in x, never leave the table for theory. Confirm on one more size, then commit.

Write the quantity asked for as a formula in named symbols, including any unknown the problem never states outright, most often a count; substitute numbers only at the end. Mark each given number as a total for a group or an amount per item.

If per-item amounts must be whole or equal, that unknown count divides every such total at once, so the candidates are the divisors of their gcd. A count the problem does state describes a grouping; it constrains the unknown count without being it.

Make each percent or ratio a multiplier on the base it acts on, then check the result against every stated condition.

For commuting same-degree polynomials, do not expand the full composition coefficient by coefficient; that exhausts your budget. Match leading and constant terms, then look for a shared symmetry. Strong ansatz: link the two maps by an affine involution, f = L(g) with L(t) = s - t, and require g(s - x) = s - g(x). That one reflection identity implies the commuting identity and collapses the unknowns to a single free parameter. Fix s from the given values at x = 0. Read the requested outputs straight from the symmetry relation rather than solving for every coefficient. If an ansatz fails, test a different symmetry instead of concluding no such polynomials exist, then verify the identity at one numeric input.

One application means the whole prescribed sequence of steps, never a single step; settle that first. Run it literally on the smallest nontrivial instance with distinct labels, writing out each state until the original returns, and count. If two of your own passes at one size disagree, a convention slipped: settle it once, keep it fixed, and move on. A composite does not inherit the period of its parts. Get one more size the same way, fit one formula in the parameter, and box it rather than listing rivals.
